topics.description: The software layer that manages hardware and provides services to programs, so applications need not address devices directly.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The core of the OS. It schedules the CPU, manages memory, drives devices, and enforces permissions. Everything else is userspace.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Privileged kernel execution versus unprivileged application execution. The boundary is what stops one program corrupting another.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The controlled entry point by which a userspace program asks the kernel to do privileged work such as opening a file.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: The program interpreting typed commands and turning them into process execution. Bash is the common default.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The interface presenting a shell. The terminal displays; the shell interprets. They are routinely conflated.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: The Unix design principle by which devices, sockets, and kernel state are all reached through the filesystem interface.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Linux runs many users and many processes concurrently, isolating each — which is why permissions and process ownership exist at all.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The kernel packaged with GNU tools, a package manager, defaults, and a release policy. The kernel alone is not a usable system.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint) using .deb and apt; Red Hat family (RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky) using .rpm and dnf; SUSE; Arch.
topics.notes: Knowing which package manager belongs to which family is commonly tested. Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Long-term-support releases freeze versions and backport fixes for years; rolling releases ship continuously. Stability against currency.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Linux is the kernel; most of the surrounding userland is GNU. This is why the combination is sometimes called GNU/Linux.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: Begun by Linus Torvalds in 1991 as a free Unix-like kernel and developed openly ever since. The Linux Foundation sponsors and hosts the work; technical direction remains with Torvalds and the kernel maintainer hierarchy.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Linux is Unix-like and largely POSIX-conformant, which is why skills and scripts port across Unix systems.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: The kernel is released under GPLv2, which is why distributions may redistribute and modify it under the same terms.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Executes instructions. Core count and architecture determine how much work runs genuinely in parallel.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Volatile working memory. When it is exhausted the system swaps to disk and slows sharply, or begins killing processes.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Persistent block devices — HDD, SSD, NVMe — that hold filesystems and survive power loss.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: x86_64 and ARM64 are the common ones. Binaries and container images are architecture-specific.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Kernel code that drives hardware, either compiled into the kernel image or built as a module that loads and unloads at runtime.
topics.notes: Corrected in stage 5 against primary documentation (https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/kbuild/kconfig-language.html); the correction survived independent adversarial review. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Low-level software embedded in a device, distinct from the operating system that runs above it.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: Graphical and command-line interfaces. Servers are usually administered by CLI because it is scriptable, remotable, and cheap in resources.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: GNOME, KDE Plasma, XFCE and others provide the graphical desktop; the choice is independent of the distribution.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The display server protocols underlying Linux graphics, Wayland being the newer replacement. Recognition-level.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: peripheral or specialist for an entry-level exam; recognition of the term is sufficient.

topics.description: Named values inherited by processes, configuring behaviour without changing code.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The ordered list of directories the shell searches for commands. Explains "command not found" for an installed program.
topics.notes: A very common cause of confusing command-not-found errors. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Identifying what a machine is: kernel version, distribution, hostname, uptime, architecture.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A command, its options (flags), and its arguments. Short options take one dash, long options two.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Man pages, --help, apropos, and info. Man pages have numbered sections; section 5 covers file formats, which is where config syntax lives.
topics.notes: Knowing man sections exist, and that section 5 documents file formats, is worth having. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: An absolute path starts at / and is unambiguous; a relative path is interpreted from the current directory.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Current directory, parent directory, and the current user’s home.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Moving around and listing contents, including hidden dotfiles which ls omits by default.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: / is the root of the filesystem, /root is the superuser’s home directory, and ~ is the current user’s home. Three different things sharing a name.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

path: creating and removing files and directories
topics.description: touch, mkdir, cp, mv, rm. rm is immediate and unrecoverable; there is no recycle bin.
topics.notes: rm -rf with a wrong path is the classic catastrophic mistake. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: cat for short files, less for paging, head and tail for the ends, tail -f to follow a growing log.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: find walks the tree live and filters on name, size, time, or permission; locate queries a prebuilt index and is faster but can be stale.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Determining what a file actually is and when it changed, rather than trusting its extension.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The file-handling command family folded into this competency in 2025: listing, copying, moving, removing, linking and inspecting files.
topics.notes: Folded in from the retired "File Management Commands" competency. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The ten-character mode string: a leading type character (- file, d directory, l symlink) then three permission triads for owner, group and other. drwxr-xr-x is a directory the owner may write and everyone may read and traverse.
topics.notes: Reading a mode string, and converting it to and from octal such as 644 or 755, is a staple multiple-choice item. Depth rationale: specific configuration syntax is itself examinable.

topics.description: Linux filenames and commands are case-sensitive: File.txt and file.txt are different files. A frequent stumbling block for people arriving from Windows.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The shell expands * ? and [] into matching filenames before the command ever runs.
topics.notes: Expansion happens in the shell, not the command — which is why quoting changes behaviour. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Double quotes preserve spacing but still expand variables; single quotes suppress all expansion; a backslash escapes one character.
topics.notes: Unquoted variables containing spaces are a frequent scripting bug. Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: ; runs sequentially regardless, && runs only on success, || runs only on failure.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Substitutes a command’s output into another command, written $(...).
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Variables are local to the shell until exported, at which point child processes inherit them.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Recalling previous commands and completing names, both of which reduce typing errors.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Short names for longer commands, defined in shell startup files.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Every command returns a status: 0 for success, non-zero for failure. It drives && and || and is how scripts detect problems.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: stdin, stdout and stderr — file descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Errors travel separately from output, which is why 2> exists.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: a named confusable pair, which is exactly the shape a multiple-choice comparison question takes.

topics.description: > writes to a file and truncates it, >> appends, < reads from a file, 2> captures errors, and /dev/null discards.
topics.notes: > silently destroys the existing contents of the target file. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Connects one command’s stdout to the next command’s stdin, letting small tools be composed. stderr is not carried by default.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Searches input for lines matching a pattern. The single most-used text tool on a Linux system.
topics.notes: grep searches inside files; find locates files. A commonly confused pair. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Pattern syntax used by grep, sed, and others. Basic anchors, character classes and quantifiers are enough at this level.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: Stream editor, most often used for search-and-replace across a file or pipeline.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Field-aware text processor, natural for columnar output such as printing the third column of a report.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Extract fields, order lines, collapse duplicates, and count. uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort usually precedes it.
topics.notes: uniq without a preceding sort is a classic mistake. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Shows differences between files, the basis of patches and code review.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: vi/vim is present on essentially every Unix system; nano is simpler. Knowing how to save and quit vi is a practical necessity.
topics.notes: Being trapped in vi is a rite of passage; :q! exits without saving. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: tar bundles many files into one archive; gzip, bzip2 and xz compress. tar czf creates a compressed archive in one step.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Moving files between hosts with scp, sftp, or rsync; rsync transfers only differences and can resume.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: A file of commands made executable, beginning with a shebang naming the interpreter.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Conditionals and loops — if, for, while — plus positional parameters for arguments.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: conceptual: explain what it is and why it exists.

topics.description: The command family folded into this competency in 2025: inspecting processes, memory, disk and uptime from the shell. The underlying concepts live under System Administration; what belongs here is knowing which command answers which question.
topics.notes: One of three command families the Linux Foundation collapsed into Command Line in the 2025 update. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Inspecting current sessions and login history, which is both an operational and a security question.
topics.notes: Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: The networking command family folded into this competency in 2025: checking addresses, reachability, name resolution and listening sockets from the shell.
topics.notes: Folded in from the retired "General Networking Commands" competency. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.

topics.description: Well-known or system ports are 0-1023 and need privilege to bind; registered ports are 1024-49151; dynamic or ephemeral ports are 49152-65535 and are used for the client end of a connection.
topics.notes: The reason a non-root process cannot bind port 80 but can bind 8080. Depth rationale: command-bearing: the exam can ask which command or option fits a stated need.
